notes.front: What is a turbine engine inlet designed to provide?
notes.back: A relatively distortion-free flow of air, in the required quantity, to the compressor inlet.
notes.explanation: Many engines also use inlet guide vanes to straighten the airflow into the first compressor stages.
notes.example: Like the air intake of a piston engine, but far larger, since a gas turbine consumes much more air.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbine Engine Inlet Systems”, p. 3-16
notes.evidence: The engine inlet of a turbine engine is designed to provide a relatively distortion-free flow of air, in the required quantity, to the inlet of the compressor. [Figure 3-24] Many engines use inlet guide vanes (IGV) to help straighten the airflow and direct it into the first stages of the compressor.

notes.front: What is a divided-entrance duct?
notes.back: An inlet duct that takes air from either side of the fuselage, as a wing-root inlet or a scoop on each side.
notes.explanation: It suits high-speed military aircraft whose pilot sits low in the fuselage close to the nose.
notes.example: Like a single nose intake split into two side scoops that join before the compressor.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Divided-Entrance Duct”, p. 3-17
notes.evidence: Some form of a divided duct, which takes air from either side of the fuselage, has become fairly widely used. This divided duct can be either a wing-root inlet or a scoop at each side of the fuselage.

notes.front: What is a variable-geometry inlet duct?
notes.back: An inlet duct on very high-speed aircraft whose internal area is changed by a mechanical device as the aircraft speeds up or slows down.
notes.explanation: Supersonic inlet air must be slowed below Mach 1 before it enters the engine.
notes.example: Like a divided-entrance duct, but with a moving ramp or wedge inside that reshapes it with speed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Variable-Geometry Duct”, p. 3-18
notes.evidence: For very high speed aircraft, the inside area of configuration of the duct is changed by a mechanical device as the speed of the aircraft increases or decreases. A duct of this type is usually known as a variable-geometry inlet duct.

notes.front: What is a compressor inlet screen?
notes.back: A screen sometimes placed across the engine air inlet, somewhere along the inlet duct, so the engine does not readily ingest objects.
notes.explanation: Engines with inlet screens, such as turboprops and APUs, are less vulnerable to foreign object damage.
notes.example: Like a guard over a household fan’s intake, stopping loose objects being drawn in.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Compressor Inlet Screens”, p. 3-18
notes.evidence: To prevent the engine from readily ingesting any items that can be drawn in the intake, a compressor inlet screen is sometimes placed across the engine air inlet at some location along the inlet duct. Engines that incorporate inlet screens, such as turboprops [Figure 3-28] and APUs [Figure 3-29] are not as vulnerable to FOD.

notes.front: What is a bellmouth inlet?
notes.back: A bell-shaped funnel with carefully rounded shoulders, usually fitted to an engine being tested in a test cell.
notes.explanation: It is designed with the single objective of very high aerodynamic efficiency, offering practically no air resistance.
notes.example: Like the flared mouth of a trumpet, turned to face forward so air slides smoothly into the engine.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Bellmouth Compressor Inlets”, p. 3-19
notes.evidence: The bellmouth is designed with the single objective of obtaining very high aerodynamic efficiency. Essentially, the inlet is a bell-shaped funnel having carefully rounded shoulders which offer practically no air resistance.

notes.front: Why is a turboprop’s air inlet more of a design problem than some other gas turbine inlets?
notes.back: The propeller drive shaft, hub and spinner must be considered as well as the other inlet design factors.
notes.explanation: The ducted arrangement is generally considered the best turboprop inlet for airflow and aerodynamics.
notes.example: Like a turbofan inlet, but with the propeller’s shaft and hub sitting right in front of it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turboprop & Turboshaft Compressor Inlets”, p. 3-19
notes.evidence: The air inlet on a turboprop is more of a problem than some other gas turbine engines because the propeller drive shaft, the hub, and the spinner must be considered in addition to other inlet design factors.

notes.front: In a high-bypass turbofan, what does the inlet section feed first?
notes.back: The fan, which is usually at the forward end of the compressor; the inlet cowl may be bolted to the engine front.
notes.explanation: Air through the outer fan forms the secondary (fan) stream; air through the inner part becomes the core flow.
notes.example: Like the turboprop inlet, but opening straight onto a large fan rather than past a propeller hub.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbofan Engine Inlet Sections”, p. 3-19
notes.evidence: High-bypass turbofan engines are usually constructed with the fan at the forward end of the compressor. A typical turbofan intake section is shown in Figure 3-34. Sometimes, the inlet cowl is bolted to the front of the engine and provides the airflow path into the engine.

notes.front: How does a gas turbine engine’s cooling differ from a reciprocating engine’s?
notes.back: Combustion is continuous, so nearly all the cooling air must pass through the inside of the engine.
notes.explanation: In a four-stroke piston engine, combustion occurs only every fourth stroke, which eases the cooling problem.
notes.example: Like cooling a stove burner that never switches off, from the inside, rather than one that fires in pulses.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Turbine Engine Cooling”, p. 6-38
notes.evidence: The cooling problem is made easier because combustion occurs only during every fourth stroke of a fourstroke-cycle engine. The burning process in a gas turbine engine is continuous, and nearly all of the cooling air must be passed through the inside of the engine.

notes.front: What is accessory zone cooling in a turbine powerplant?
notes.back: Supplying calibrated airflows to zones isolated by fireproof bulkheads and seals, keeping temperatures acceptable and venting harmful vapours.
notes.explanation: The zones named are the fan case compartment, the intermediate compressor case compartment and the core engine compartment.
notes.example: Like ventilating separate rooms of a building, each sealed from the next by a fire door.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Accessory Zone Cooling”, p. 6-38
notes.evidence: The zones are the fan case compartment, intermediate compressor case compartment, and the core engine compartment. [Figure 6-61] Calibrated airflows are supplied to the zones to keep the temperatures around the engine at levels that are acceptable. The airflow provides for proper ventilation to prevent a buildup of any harmful vapors.

notes.front: What is a turbine engine insulation blanket for?
notes.back: To lower structure temperatures near the exhaust duct or afterburner and keep fuel or oil from touching hot engine parts.
notes.explanation: It is fitted on the exhaust duct, whose surface temperature runs quite high.
notes.example: Like lagging around a hot water pipe, but wrapped round a jet exhaust duct.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Turbine Engine Insulation Blankets”, p. 6-40
notes.evidence: To reduce the temperature of the structure in the vicinity of the exhaust duct or thrust augmentor (afterburner) and to eliminate the possibility of fuel or oil coming in contact with the hot parts of the engine, it is sometimes necessary to provide insulation on the exhaust duct of gas turbine engines.

notes.front: How is the inlet of a modern turbofan protected from ice?
notes.back: Warm air is bled from the compressor and ducted through the inlet to prevent ice forming.
notes.explanation: Ice on the inlet leading edge could break loose and damage the fan, which is the first part the incoming air meets.
notes.example: Like a heated car windscreen edge, but warmed by air tapped from the engine’s own compressor.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Engines, “Air Entrance”, p. 1-37
notes.evidence: This prevents chunks of ice from forming on the leading edge of the inlet, breaking loose, and damaging the fan. Warm air is bled from the engine’s compressor and is ducted through the inlet to prevent ice from forming.

notes.front: What is thermal anti-icing?
notes.back: A system that prevents ice forming on an aircraft by flowing heated air inside the structure.
notes.explanation: On business jets and large transports, the heated air is typically hot bleed air from the engine compressor.
notes.example: Like underfloor heating, but warming the inside of a leading edge so ice cannot form on it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Glossary, Glossary
notes.evidence: TAI. Thermal anti-ice. A system used to prevent the formation of ice on an aircraft by flowing heated air inside the structure.

notes.front: A damaged inlet duct delivers turbulent, uneven air to a turbine engine’s compressor. Which problems does the handbook link to non-uniform inlet airflow?
notes.back: B) Compressor stall and excessive internal temperatures in the turbine section
notes.choices:
A) None: inlet ducts are airframe parts and do not affect the engine
B) Compressor stall and excessive internal temperatures in the turbine section
C) Only higher fuel flow at idle
D) Only extra noise from the fan
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: although the duct is an airframe part, it is very important to engine performance. C and D are not the effects the handbook names.
notes.explanation: A uniform and steady airflow is necessary to avoid both problems.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbine Engine Inlet Systems”, p. 3-16
notes.evidence: A uniform and steady airflow is necessary to avoid compressor stall (airflow tends to stop or reverse direction of flow) and excessive internal engine temperatures in the turbine section.

notes.front: Normally, a turbine engine’s air-inlet duct is considered {{c1::an airframe part}} and not part of the engine.
notes.explanation: Even so, the duct is very important to the engine’s overall performance and its ability to produce thrust.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbine Engine Inlet Systems”, p. 3-16
notes.evidence: Normally, the air-inlet duct is considered an airframe part and not a part of the engine. However, the duct is very important to the engine’s overall performance and the engine’s ability to produce an optimum amount of thrust.

notes.front: What do turbine inlet ducts do to the air passing through them?
notes.back: They act as diffusers with a divergent shape, decreasing the air’s velocity and increasing its static pressure.
notes.explanation: The duct must also deliver air uniformly with little turbulence and hold drag to a minimum.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbine Engine Inlet Systems”, p. 3-17
notes.evidence: To accomplish this, inlet ducts are designed to function as diffusers with a divergent shape, decreasing the velocity and increasing the static pressure of the air passing through them.

notes.front: Airflow through a turbine engine must be {{c1::less than Mach 1}} at all times, so supersonic inlet air must be slowed in the duct.
notes.explanation: This is why supersonic military inlet ducts first converge, then diverge as subsonic diffusers.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Variable-Geometry Duct”, p. 3-17
notes.evidence: Airflow through the engine must be less than Mach 1 at all times. Therefore, under all flight conditions, the velocity of the airflow as it enters the air-inlet duct must be reduced through the duct before the airflow is ready to enter the compressor.

notes.front: What three methods do military aircraft use to slow supersonic inlet air?
notes.back: A movable ramp or wedge varying duct area; a variable airflow bypass ahead of the engine; and a deliberately set-up shock wave.
notes.explanation: In at least one installation, the device that changes the duct area also sets up the shock wave.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Variable-Geometry Duct”, p. 3-18
notes.evidence: One is to vary the area, or geometry, of the inlet duct either by using a movable restriction, such as a ramp or wedge, inside the duct. Another system is some sort of a variable airflow bypass arrangement, which extracts part of the inlet airflow from the duct ahead of the engine.

notes.front: An engine has an axial compressor fitted with aluminium compressor blades. What does the handbook say about an inlet screen for it?
notes.back: D) A screen is almost a necessity
notes.choices:
A) Screens are never used on axial compressors
B) A screen should be fitted only for test-cell runs
C) A screen is pointless, since screens ice up
D) A screen is almost a necessity
notes.choicesExplained: A and B have no basis in the handbook. C overstates a drawback: screens are susceptible to icing, but for this engine the handbook still calls one almost a necessity.
notes.explanation: An engine readily subject to internal damage, such as one with aluminium blades, benefits most from a screen.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Compressor Inlet Screens”, p. 3-18
notes.evidence: If the engine is readily subjected to internal damage, as would be the case for an engine having an axial compressor fitted with aluminum compressor blades, an inlet screen is almost a necessity.

notes.front: What are the drawbacks of compressor inlet screens?
notes.back: They add appreciably to inlet pressure loss, are very susceptible to icing, and can fail from fatigue.
notes.explanation: A failed screen can sometimes cause more damage than no screen at all.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Compressor Inlet Screens”, p. 3-18
notes.evidence: Screens, however, add appreciably to inlet duct pressure loss and are very susceptible to icing. Failure due to fatigue is also a problem. A failed screen can sometimes cause more damage than no screen at all.

notes.front: Why are compressor inlet screens not generally used on large turbofan engines?
notes.back: Their steel or titanium fan blades do not damage easily, so the screens’ disadvantages outweigh their advantages.
notes.explanation: Screens are more common on turboprops and APUs.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Compressor Inlet Screens”, p. 3-19
notes.evidence: easily, the disadvantages of compressor screens outweigh the advantages, so they are not generally used.

notes.front: Why is engine performance data, such as rated thrust and thrust specific fuel consumption, obtained with a bellmouth inlet?
notes.back: Its duct loss is so slight that it is considered zero, so the engine runs free of installed-inlet losses.
notes.explanation: The bellmouth is fitted with probes that measure intake temperature and pressure during testing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Bellmouth Compressor Inlets”, p. 3-19
notes.evidence: Duct loss is so slight that it is considered zero. The engine can, therefore, be operated without the complications resulting from losses common to an installed aircraft inlet duct. Engine performance data, such as rated thrust and thrust specific fuel consumption, are obtained while using a bellmouth inlet.

notes.front: A test-cell bellmouth is fitted with a protective screen, and very accurate engine data are needed. What must be done?
notes.back: D) Account for the efficiency lost as air passes through the screen
notes.choices:
A) Remove the screen and run without protection
B) Nothing: bellmouth losses are always zero
C) Fit an aircraft inlet duct instead
D) Account for the efficiency lost as air passes through the screen
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores the screen loss. C would add the installed-duct losses the bellmouth avoids. A is wrong because bellmouths are usually fitted with protective screens, and the handbook has the screen loss accounted for rather than the screen removed.
notes.explanation: Bellmouth inlets are usually fitted with protective screening, which costs some efficiency.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Bellmouth Compressor Inlets”, p. 3-19
notes.evidence: Usually, the inlets are fitted with protective screening. In this case, the efficiency lost as the air passes through the screen must be taken into account when very accurate engine data are necessary.

notes.front: How are the inlets of many turboprops anti-iced?
notes.back: By electrical elements in the lip opening of the intake.
notes.explanation: Ducting in the engine or nacelle then directs the airflow to the engine intake.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turboprop & Turboshaft Compressor Inlets”, p. 3-19
notes.evidence: The inlet for many types of turboprops are anti-iced by using electrical elements in the lip opening of the intake.

notes.front: A turboprop operates from gravel strips in winter. Which inlet feature does the handbook describe for keeping ice or dirt out of the intake?
notes.back: C) Deflector doors that deflect ice or dirt away from the intake
notes.choices:
A) A bellmouth inlet
B) A variable-geometry inlet duct
C) Deflector doors that deflect ice or dirt away from the intake
D) An abradable rub strip
notes.choicesExplained: A is for test cells. B slows supersonic air. D lets fan blades rub briefly inside a turbofan inlet.
notes.explanation: On some models the air then passes through a screen before entering the engine.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turboprop & Turboshaft Compressor Inlets”, p. 3-19
notes.evidence: Deflector doors are sometimes used to deflect ice or dirt away from the intake. [Figure 3-33] The air then passes through a screen and into the engine on some models.

notes.front: How does the fan of a high-bypass turbofan reduce damage from ingested foreign material?
notes.back: Much of the material is thrown radially outward and leaves through the fan discharge rather than the engine core.
notes.explanation: The fan also permits a conventional inlet duct with low inlet duct loss.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbofan Engine Inlet Sections”, p. 3-20
notes.evidence: The fan reduces engine damage from ingested foreign material because much of any material that may be ingested is thrown radially outward and passes through the fan discharge rather than through the core of the engine.

notes.front: What is the abradable rub strip inside a turbofan inlet for?
notes.back: It lets the fan blade tips rub for short times during flightpath changes.
notes.explanation: Sound-reducing materials inside the inlet lower the noise the fan generates.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbofan Engine Inlet Sections”, p. 3-20
notes.evidence: Inside the inlet by the fan blade tips is an abraidable rub strip that allows the fan blades to rub for short times due to flightpath changes.

notes.front: Warm bleed air circulates inside a turbofan’s inlet lip to stop ice forming. Which ice control method is this?
notes.back: D) Thermal pneumatic anti-icing
notes.choices:
A) Pneumatic deicing boots
B) Thermal electric anti-icing
C) Chemical anti-icing
D) Thermal pneumatic anti-icing
notes.choicesExplained: A removes ice after it forms, using inflatable boots. C uses fluid. B uses electrical heating elements, as in many turboprop inlet lips.
notes.explanation: The Airframe handbook lists thermal pneumatic and thermal electric as the methods for engine air inlets.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 3, Induction & Exhaust Systems, “Turbofan Engine Inlet Sections”, p. 3-20
notes.evidence: Warm bleed air is drawn from the engine and circulated on the inside of the inlet lip for anti-icing.

notes.front: Which ice control methods does the Airframe handbook list for heater and engine air inlets?
notes.back: Thermal pneumatic and thermal electric.
notes.explanation: Chemical and pneumatic deicing are listed for other areas, such as wing leading edges.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 15, Ice & Rain Protection, “Ice Prevention”, p. 15-3
notes.evidence: Heater and engine air inlets Thermal pneumatic and thermal electric

notes.front: How does anti-icing equipment differ from deicing equipment in when it is used?
notes.back: Anti-icing is turned on before entering icing conditions, to prevent ice; deicing removes ice after it begins to accumulate.
notes.explanation: A surface may be anti-iced by keeping it dry, or by heating it just enough to prevent freezing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 15, Ice & Rain Protection, “Ice Prevention”, p. 15-3
notes.evidence: Anti-icing equipment is turned on before entering icing conditions and is designed to prevent ice from forming.

notes.front: How can leaks be found in bleed-air anti-icing ducting, and what must its lagging be free of?
notes.back: Often by ear or holes in the lagging, else with soap and water; lagging must be free of flammable fluids such as oil.
notes.explanation: Ducts are also pressure tested when specified, and leakage must not exceed the maintenance manual’s rate.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 15, Ice & Rain Protection, “Thermal Pneumatic Anti-icing”, p. 15-5
notes.evidence: Air leaks can often be detected audibly and are sometimes revealed by holes in the lagging or thermal insulation material. However, if difficulty arises in locating leaks, a soap-andwater solution may be used.

notes.front: Why is a large surplus of air, beyond the ideal 15:1 air-fuel ratio, admitted to a gas turbine?
notes.back: At 15:1 alone, internal temperatures would exceed 4,000 °F; the surplus cools hot sections to about 1,500–2,100 °F.
notes.explanation: The hottest area is in and around the turbines.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Turbine Engine Cooling”, p. 6-38
notes.evidence: If only enough air were admitted to the engine to provide an ideal air-fuel ratio of 15:1, internal temperatures would increase to more than 4,000 °F. In practice, a large amount of air in excess of the ideal ratio is admitted to the engine.

notes.front: How does secondary air cool combustion-chamber liners?
notes.back: The liners are built to induce a thin, fast-moving film of air over both their inner and outer surfaces.
notes.explanation: Relatively cool air also mixes with the burned gases aft of the burners, just before the turbines.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Turbine Engine Cooling”, p. 6-38
notes.evidence: The secondary air passing through the engine cools the combustion-chamber liners. The liners are constructed to induce a thin, fast-moving film of air over both the inner and outer surfaces of the liner.

notes.front: A turbine engine compartment is frequently divided into a forward {{c1::cold section}} and an aft (turbine) hot section.
notes.explanation: The engine exterior and nacelle are cooled by passing fan air around them.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Turbine Engine Cooling”, p. 6-38
notes.evidence: The engine compartment frequently is divided into two sections. The forward section is referred to as the cold section and the aft section (turbine) is referred to as the hot section.

notes.front: What feature of a turbine engine installation stops leaking fluids building up in the nacelle?
notes.back: A) Case drains that drain potential leaks overboard
notes.choices:
A) Case drains that drain potential leaks overboard
B) The bellmouth inlet
C) The insulation blanket, which absorbs them
D) The compressor inlet screen
notes.choicesExplained: C is wrong: blankets are covered so they do not become oil-soaked. B and D are inlet features unrelated to nacelle fluids.
notes.explanation: Air vented into or from the engine, by contrast, is ejected into the exhaust stream.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Turbine Engine Cooling”, p. 6-38
notes.evidence: Case drains drain potential leaks overboard to prevent fluids from building up in the nacelle.

notes.front: In the handbook’s zone cooling example, what happens if pressure in Zone 1, around the fan case, exceeds a set limit?
notes.back: A) A pressure relief door opens and relieves the pressure
notes.choices:
A) A pressure relief door opens and relieves the pressure
B) The thrust reverser deploys
C) Fan air is shut off to the zone
D) The engine is shut down automatically
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D are not described for Zone 1; the handbook names only the pressure relief door.
notes.explanation: Zone 1 holds the accessory case and the electronic engine control, and is vented by ram air through a nose-cowl inlet.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Accessory Zone Cooling”, p. 6-38
notes.evidence: This area is vented by using ram air through an inlet in the nose cowl and is exhausted through a louvered vent in the right fan cowling. If the pressure exceeds a certain limit, a pressure relief door opens and relieves the pressure.

notes.front: In the handbook’s example, how is Zone 2 cooled, and why is removing vapours there important?
notes.back: By fan air from the upper fan duct, exhausted back into the fan stream; the zone contains fuel and oil lines.
notes.explanation: Zone 3, around the high-pressure compressor to the turbine cases, also holds fuel and oil lines.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Accessory Zone Cooling”, p. 6-38
notes.evidence: Zone 2 is cooled by fan air from the upper part of the fan duct and is exhausted at the lower end back into the fan air stream. This area has both

notes.front: What separates the primary zones of a turbine powerplant from each other?
notes.back: Fireproof bulkheads and seals.
notes.explanation: The Airman Certification Standards list turbine engine baffle and seal installation as knowledge for this subject.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Accessory Zone Cooling”, p. 6-38
notes.evidence: Turbine powerplants can be divided into primary zones that are isolated from each other by fireproof bulkheads and seals.

notes.front: In a typical turbine insulation blanket, what are the low-conductance material and the radiation shield?
notes.back: Fibreglass is the low-conductance material and aluminium foil the radiation shield.
notes.explanation: The blanket is covered so that it does not become oil-soaked.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Turbine Engine Insulation Blankets”, p. 6-40
notes.evidence: This blanket contains fiberglass as the low conductance material and aluminum foil as the radiation shield. The blanket is suitably covered so that it does not become oil soaked.

notes.front: A transport aircraft has a long exhaust duct running close to structure and to fuel and oil lines. Which feature protects them?
notes.back: D) An insulation blanket on the exhaust duct
notes.choices:
A) A compressor inlet screen
B) An abradable rub strip
C) A bellmouth inlet
D) An insulation blanket on the exhaust duct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are inlet features and do nothing for exhaust duct heat.
notes.explanation: Blankets have been used extensively where a long exhaust is needed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Turbine Engine Insulation Blankets”, p. 6-40
notes.evidence: Insulation blankets have been used rather extensively on many installations in which long exhaust is needed.

notes.front: What does internal cooling air, bled from the compressor, cool inside a turbine engine?
notes.back: The turbine disc, vanes and blades, and sometimes the turbine bearing.
notes.explanation: Bleed air over the turbine disc also reduces heat radiation to the bearing surface.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Turbine Engine Lubrication Systems”, p. 6-21
notes.evidence: This internal air flow has many uses on the inside of the engine. It is used to cool turbine disc, vanes, and blades. Also, some turbine wheels may have bleed air flowing over the turbine disc, which reduces heat radiation to the bearing surface.

notes.front: From which compressor stage is bearing and disc cooling air usually bled?
notes.back: C) A stage where the air has enough pressure but has not yet become too warm
notes.choices:
A) Always the final, highest-pressure stage
B) The fan bypass duct only
C) A stage where the air has enough pressure but has not yet become too warm
D) The turbine exhaust
notes.choicesExplained: A gives the hottest air. B and D are not compressor stages.
notes.explanation: The handbook notes that air becomes heated as it is compressed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 6, Lubrication & Cooling Systems, “Turbine Engine Lubrication Systems”, p. 6-21
notes.evidence: This bleed air, as it is called, is usually bled off a compressor stage at a point where air has enough pressure but has not yet become too warm (as the air is compressed, it becomes heated).

notes.front: What are two current applications of compressor bleed air that the handbook lists?
notes.back: Any two of: cabin pressurisation, heating and cooling; deicing and anti-icing; pneumatic engine starting; auxiliary drive units.
notes.explanation: The bleed port’s stage is chosen for the pressure or temperature the job needs.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-32B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Engines, “Compressor Section”, p. 1-38
notes.evidence: Some of the current applications of bleed air are: 1. Cabin pressurization, heating, and cooling; 2. Deicing and anti-icing equipment; 3. Pneumatic starting of engines; and 4. Auxiliary drive units (ADU).

notes.front: Which two risks do the Airman Certification Standards name for turbine engine air systems?
notes.back: Maintenance on compressor bleed air systems, and ground operation of engines other than by the manufacturer’s instructions.
notes.explanation: The same subject lists inspecting and checking a bleed air system as a skill.
notes.source: FAA-S-ACS-1, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (2021), Section III, Subject K, Turbine Engine Air Systems, p. 57
notes.evidence: AM.III.K.R1 Maintenance on compressor bleed air systems. AM.III.K.R2 Ground operation of aircraft engines following other than manufacturer's instructions.
